title: This Atlantic hurricane season is about to do something that hasn't happened in 175 years
gist: The 2026 Atlantic basin has passed its September 10 climatological peak without a single hurricane, on track to beat the 1941 record for latest first hurricane, with accumulated cyclone energy at 7 percent of normal and ranking 77th of 77 years since 1950. The cause is an exceptionally strong El Niño — nearly 3°C above baseline, the strongest observed at this time of year in the modern record — whose wind shear suppresses Atlantic storms but is already cutting Panama Canal rainfall and is expected to make 2027 the planet's hottest year on record.

themes.theme: A record-breaking absence of Atlantic hurricanes

insights.claim: The Atlantic basin passed its traditional seasonal peak around September 10 in 2026 without a single tropical wave, storm or hurricane present.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Peak season passing empty removes the largest single seasonal risk premium from Gulf energy and US property-catastrophe exposure.
insights.quote: Last week, the Atlantic hurricane season blew through its traditional peak—which comes around September 10—with nary a tropical wave in sight
insights.locator: Last week, the Atlantic hurricane season blew through its traditional peak

insights.claim: Since aircraft monitoring of the Atlantic basin began in 1944, a hurricane had formed every single year by September 11 without exception.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: An 82-year streak breaking is a genuine tail event, useful for recalibrating catastrophe models that assume peak-season activity is near-certain.

insights.claim: The latest previous first Atlantic hurricanes in the aircraft-monitoring era were Gustav in 2002 and Humberto in 2013, both arriving around September 11.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: These are the comparables analysts should pull to model how quiet-start seasons resolved in October and November.
insights.locator: The latest “first” Atlantic hurricanes came in 2002, with Gustav

insights.claim: Extending records back to 1851, every year has produced at least one Atlantic hurricane, and the latest first hurricane on record formed on September 17, 1941.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: September 17 is the concrete date to watch as the record-break threshold and a marker of regime change in Atlantic activity.
insights.quote: But in 1941, the first hurricane did not form until September 17. This is the date of the latest first Atlantic hurricane on record.
insights.locator: Atlantic hurricane records officially go back to 1851

insights.claim: Pre-1944 Atlantic hurricane records are less reliable because storm detection depended on reports from shipping vessels, meaning some storms were simply missed.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Any long-run trend claim built on pre-1944 hurricane counts carries an undercount bias that flatters historical quiet periods.
insights.locator: Atlantic hurricane records officially go back to 1851

insights.claim: The 2026 Atlantic accumulated cyclone energy ranks 77th out of 77 years of data going back to 1950, at just 7 percent of normal levels, generated by only five relatively weak tropical storms.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Dead-last ACE at 7 percent of normal implies a near-total miss for the reinsurance loss year and should show up in cat-bond and reinsurer results.
insights.quote: this year’s accumulated cyclone energy ranks 77th out of 77 years, with a value of just 7 percent of normal levels
insights.locator: By other measures, this season is also extraordinarily quiet

themes.theme: Near-term forecast and remaining season risk

insights.claim: The forecaster states flatly that the Atlantic will not produce a hurricane by the end of Thursday, with the National Hurricane Center giving its single monitored disturbance a near-zero chance of even becoming a tropical depression within two days.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A near-certain quiet window through mid-September removes the immediate catalyst for Gulf energy supply disruption trades.
insights.quote: I’m here to tell you that the Atlantic will not produce a hurricane by the end of Thursday.
insights.locator: I’m here to tell you that the Atlantic will not produce a hurricane

insights.claim: The Atlantic season officially runs to the end of November and often produces hurricanes in October, so a completely hurricane-free year remains too early to call even after a record-quiet peak.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Do not close hurricane hedges yet — roughly ten weeks of season remain and October activity is historically common.
insights.quote: the odds are rising, and that would be historic
insights.locator: The Atlantic season still has some runway left

insights.claim: Even hurricanes that never make landfall can send energy prices skyrocketing when they form in the Gulf of Mexico, so the absence of storms is itself a price-suppressing factor.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: The hurricane risk premium normally embedded in Gulf-linked natural gas and refined product prices has had no trigger this year.
insights.quote: Even storms at sea, in the Gulf of Mexico, can send energy prices skyrocketing—the last thing needed this year.

themes.theme: El Niño as the suppressing mechanism

insights.claim: A strengthening El Niño in the Pacific Ocean is the direct cause of the Atlantic's quiet season, producing hostile wind shear over the basin's main development region that has been measured this year.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: As long as El Niño holds, Atlantic hurricane risk stays structurally suppressed — a tradeable persistence signal, not a random quiet year.
insights.quote: a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific Ocean has put the kibosh on the main development region of the Atlantic this year
insights.locator: Take the good with the bad

insights.claim: This summer's El Niño anomaly of nearly 3°C above baseline in the Pacific is stronger than any observed at this time of year in the modern record.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A record-strength anomaly implies record-scale downstream effects on agriculture, shipping and temperature — size the second-order trades to the anomaly, not to history.
insights.quote: The El Niño anomaly this summer, nearly 3° C above baseline in the Pacific, is stronger than any observed at this time of year in the modern record.
insights.locator: Take the good with the bad

insights.claim: The Atlantic's main development region is additionally choked with Saharan dust on top of the wind shear, a second suppressing factor operating simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Two independent suppressors reduce the chance of a late-season regime flip more than wind shear alone would.
insights.locator: But this year, the main region where most tropical systems develop is choked with Saharan dust

insights.claim: The season is anomalous because tropical sea surface temperatures typically peak at this time of year, meaning the suppression is atmospheric rather than a lack of ocean heat.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Ocean heat content remains loaded, so any collapse in shear could produce rapid intensification with little warning.
insights.locator: Usually this is the time of year when sea surface temperatures reach their warmest

themes.theme: Second-order El Niño damage: canal, crops, heat

insights.claim: On balance El Niño will be far more disruptive than beneficial when it peaks this fall and winter, with the Atlantic hurricane quiet being the exception rather than the rule.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Net-net, treat the quiet hurricane season as a small offset against much larger El Niño costs elsewhere in the global economy.
insights.quote: But on balance, El Niño will probably be far more disruptive than beneficial when it peaks this fall and winter
insights.locator: This clearly is having some benefit in the tropical Atlantic

insights.claim: Diminished rains from El Niño are already affecting travel through the Panama Canal.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Canal transit restrictions raise container and LNG shipping costs and rerouting risk — a live freight-rate catalyst already in motion.
insights.locator: with diminished rains already impacting travel through the Panama Canal

insights.claim: El Niño could lead to poor rice harvests in Asia and famine elsewhere as it peaks.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Rice supply shocks feed export bans and food inflation in importing emerging markets; watch Asian rice export policy into the winter.
insights.locator: possibly leading to poor rice harvests in Asia and famine elsewhere

insights.claim: Because El Niño's effect on global temperatures typically lags by several months, 2027 is almost assuredly going to be the planet's hottest year on record with a brutal Northern Hemisphere summer.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A pre-announced record-heat year sets up 2027 demand for cooling power, grid stress and agricultural stress trades roughly a year ahead.
insights.quote: Almost assuredly, 2027 will be the planet’s hottest year on record
insights.locator: And then there is El Niño’s impact on global temperatures
